The Battle of the Nile. Also called the Battle of Aboukir Bay, this naval defeat took place on August 1, 1798, in Aboukir Bay near the mouth of the Nile River. British Admiral Horatio Nelson's fleet of 13 ships destroyed most of the French squadron of 13 ships of the line plus supporting vessels, supporting Napoleon's Egyptian campaign. The loss isolated the French expeditionary force and ultimately forced its withdrawal. Napoleon had invaded Egypt in 1798 to strike at British interests. The French fleet under Admiral Brueys anchored in a shallow defensive formation in the bay. Nelson's fleet attacked both sides of the French line simultaneously, a daring tactic that achieved local superiority and prevented the French from concentrating their firepower. The French flagship L'Orient, a massive 120-gun ship, caught fire and exploded, killing Admiral Brueys and triggering a general British victory throughout the engagement. French losses were enormous: 11 ships captured, 2 sunk, over 3,000 killed and 2,000 captured. British losses were approximately 1,800 killed and wounded across the fleet. The destruction of French naval power in the Mediterranean left Napoleon's army in Egypt stranded and forced its withdrawal by 1801. The victory established Nelson as a national hero in Britain and demonstrated that French naval power could be decisively defeated even in distant waters.
